blocks.text: The Responses API is a newer, unified interface OpenAI offers as an alternative to Chat Completions, covered in the previous topic, offering a simpler input and output structure, built-in tools without manual wiring, and optional managed conversation state.

This topic covers the simpler structure the Responses API uses, its built-in tools, how it manages conversation state differently than Chat Completions, and a practical framework for choosing between the two.
1. What the Responses API Is

blocks.alt: Building on Chat Completions, the Responses API offers a newer, unified interface

blocks.text: The Responses API is a newer endpoint OpenAI introduced, designed around a simpler request and response structure and with built-in support for certain tools, positioned as a more modern, unified alternative to the established Chat Completions endpoint covered in the previous topic.
2. A Simpler Input and Output Structure

blocks.alt: A simple input field and a simple output field structure the interaction

blocks.text: Where Chat Completions structures a request around the messages array covered in the previous topic, the Responses API simplifies this to an input field carrying the request and an output field carrying the result, reducing some of the boilerplate needed for straightforward cases.

code.content:
response = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-4",
    input="Explain recursion simply.",
)
print(response.output_text)

blocks.text: 3. Built-In Tools Without Manual Wiring

blocks.alt: Web search, file search, and code interpreter are all built in, with no manual wiring needed

blocks.text: This connects directly to tool selection and tool execution, both covered in the earlier Agent Prompting module, the Responses API offers certain tools, web search, file search, code interpreter, as built-in capabilities you can simply enable, rather than manually implementing the tool definition and execution logic yourself.

blocks.text: 4. Managing Conversation State

blocks.alt: A previous_response_id lets conversation state be managed for you

blocks.text: This connects directly to the stateless design covered in the earlier API Architecture topic, the Responses API offers a previous_response_id parameter, letting the provider manage conversation continuation for you in certain cases, rather than your application always needing to resend the entire message history manually.
5. Responses API vs Chat Completions

blocks.alt: Chat Completions requires you to resend full history, the Responses API can manage state for you

blocks.text: This is the central practical difference beyond structure, Chat Completions requires your application to reconstruct and resend the full conversation history on every call, exactly the stateless pattern covered in an earlier module, the Responses API offers an option to let the provider track that continuation instead.
6. Migrating From Chat Completions

blocks.alt: Existing Chat Completions code gets gradually migrated as needed

blocks.text: An application already built on Chat Completions does not need to migrate immediately, both endpoints remain available and well supported, migrating specific features that would genuinely benefit from built-in tools or managed state is a reasonable, incremental approach rather than an all-or-nothing rewrite.

blocks.title: Both endpoints coexist rather than one replacing the other outright
blocks.content: Chat Completions remains a fully supported, widely used endpoint, choosing between the two is a genuine design decision based on your specific needs, not simply adopting whichever is newest.

blocks.text: 7. A Worked Responses API Example

A research assistant needing current information can enable the built-in web search tool through the Responses API directly, rather than implementing a custom search tool integration manually, covered in the earlier Tool Selection Prompts and Tool Execution Prompts topics, for this specific, common need.
8. When to Prefer the Responses API

blocks.alt: Simple text generation works fine with either, built-in tools genuinely needed favors the Responses API

blocks.text: For simple text generation without special tool needs, either endpoint works reasonably well, when a feature genuinely needs one of the built-in tools the Responses API offers directly, choosing it over manually implementing the equivalent tool with Chat Completions saves real implementation effort.
9. This Sets Up Streaming Responses

The next topic in this module, Streaming Responses, covers how streaming, covered generally in an earlier module, actually works specifically with OpenAI API, applicable to both Chat Completions and the Responses API covered here.
Worked Example

A team building a research assistant initially implements a custom web search tool integration using Chat Completions, requiring meaningful implementation effort to define the tool, execute the actual search, and feed results back into the conversation, exactly the pattern covered in the earlier Agent Prompting module.

Switching this specific feature to the Responses API and enabling its built-in web search tool eliminates most of that custom implementation work, letting the team focus their effort on their actual application logic rather than reimplementing a capability the provider already offers directly.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming the Responses API entirely replaces Chat Completions rather than existing as an alternative with different tradeoffs
Manually implementing a tool the Responses API already offers as a built-in capability
Migrating an entire existing Chat Completions application at once instead of incrementally where it genuinely benefits
Not understanding the conversation state management difference before choosing between the two endpoints

blocks.text: Practice

Take a feature you have built or could build using Chat Completions that would benefit from a built-in tool like web search, sketch out how much implementation effort the Responses API built-in version would save compared to a custom tool integration.
Key Takeaway

The Responses API offers a simpler input and output structure, built-in tools like web search and code interpreter without manual implementation, and optional managed conversation state, existing alongside Chat Completions as a genuine alternative rather than a full replacement, worth choosing specifically when its built-in capabilities directly match a real application need.
